In Sections 3 and 4, we studied the model without an external instruction ($I = 0$). In this section, we will explore how the preference behaves with a positive instruction ($I = 0.70$).

The model becomes: 

$$\boxed{\dot{x} = 1.2x - 0.8x^3 + 0.70}$$

The same graphical method in Section 3.

```{python}
#|label: cue-vector
#| fig-cap: "The rate of change for $I = 0.70$. Filled points show the real equilibrium ($x\approx+1.450$). Red arrows show the direction of change on either side." 

# 1. Calculate the rate of change and equilibrium for I = 0.70

I_pos =  0.70 # define the positive instruction value
x_values = np.linspace(-2, 2, 400) # generate 400 equally spaced x values
eq_values = equilibrium_points(I_pos)  # Use the function from Section 3 to find only the real equilibria

# 2. Plot the curve and the equilibrium 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4)) # create a figure and axis object
ax.plot(x_values, f(x_values, I_pos), label = "f(x) = 1.2x - 0.8x³ + 0.70") # plot the rate of change function using the x values and positive instruction defined above
ax.axhline(0, color='black', lw=0.8, linestyle='--') # plot horizontal line at y=0 to indicate where the rate of change is zero
ax.scatter(eq_values, np.zeros(len(eq_values)), color = 'black', label = "Stable equilibrium", zorder = 3) # plot the equilibrium point(s) on the graph

# 3. Add arrows to on each side of the equilibrium to show stability
for x_test in [1.15, 1.75]: # one test point in each of the 2 regions
  direction = np.sign(f(x_test, I_pos)) # +1: right, -1: left
  ax.annotate("", xy=(x_test + 0.25 * direction, 0), # 0.25 is the length of the arrow
              xytext=(x_test - 0.25 * direction, 0),
              arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='red')) # add arrows to indicate the direction of change

# 4. Add labels showing the sign of f(x) on each side of the equilibrium
ax.text(0.9, 0.3, r"f(x) > 0", ha="center")
ax.text(1.8, 0.3, r"f(x) < 0", ha="center")

# 5. Add labels and legend
ax.set_xlabel("Coordination preference (x)") 
ax.set_ylabel(r"Rate of change $\dot{x}$") 
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
plt.show() 

print (eq_values) # only one real equilibrium is calculated
```

@fig-cue-vector shows the rate of change for $x$ between $-2$ and $2$. The curve crosses the horizontal axis only once, at $x\approx+1.450$. This is the only real equilibrium. To determine its stability, we test one point on each side of the eqilibrium to see whether $f(x)$ is positive or negative. As mention previously, since $f(x)$ is continuous and has no other equilibria, its sign stays the same within each of the two regions ($x<1.450$ and $x>1.450$). Therefore testing one point in each region is sufficient to determine stability. 

The red arrows indicate the equilibrium is stable. To the left, $f(x)>0$, so the preference $x$ increases towards equilibrium. To the right, $f(x)<0$, so the preference $x$ decreases towards it. Unlike the case $I=0$, there is no longer a stable equilibroum favouring Pattern A.

We repeat the Euler simulations from Section 4, but now with $I = 0.70$. The time step ($h=0.01$), simulation time ($t=0$ to $20$), and initial preferences ($x(0)=-1.8$ and $x(0)=+1.8$) remain the same. We use the same function `f(x, I)` and Euler formula as in Section 4. 

```{python}
# 1. Prepare the arrays using the time values from Section 4
x_A_values = np.zeros(n_steps + 1) # create empty array for starting value -1.8
x_B_values = np.zeros(n_steps + 1) # create empty array for starting value +1.8
x_A_values[0] = -1.8 # define the first value for the first array
x_B_values[0] = +1.8 # define the first value for the second array

# 2. Apply the Euler method for I = 0.70
for n in range(n_steps): # run the loop 2000 times 
  x_A_values[n + 1] = x_A_values[n] + h * f(x_A_values[n], I_pos)
  x_B_values[n + 1] = x_B_values[n] + h * f(x_B_values[n], I_pos)

# 3. Display the results
print("Final preference from -1.8:", round(x_A_values[-1], 4))
print("Final preference from +1.8:", round(x_B_values[-1], 4))
```

```{python}
# 4. Plot both trajectories and the equilibrium
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4)) # create a figure and axis

ax.plot(t, x_A_values, color = "tab:blue", label = "x(0) = -1.8")
ax.plot(t, x_B_values, color = "tab:orange", label = "x(0) = +1.8")

ax.axhline(eq_values[0], color="black", lw=0.8, ls = "--") # add horizontal line at the equilibrium
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8) # add horizontal line at y=0

ax.scatter([t0, t0], [x_A_values[0], x_B_values[0]], color = ["tab:blue" ,"tab:orange"], zorder=3, clip_on=False) # add points for the starting values

# 5. Set the y-ticks to show the starting values and the equilibrium
ticks = [x_A_values[0], 0, eq_values[0], x_B_values[0]] # define the y-ticks to show the starting values and the equilibrium
ax.set_yticks(ticks) # set the y-ticks to the defined values

# 6. Add labels and legend
ax.set_xlabel("Time (t) dimensionless")
ax.set_ylabel("Coordination preference (x)")
ax.set_xlim(t0, t_end)
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
plt.show()
```

As show in @fig-cue-trajectories, both trajectories approach the same psoitive equilibrium, $x\approx+1.450$. The preference starting at $+1.8$ decreases directly towards it. The preference starting at $-1.8$ first increases while still favouring Pattern A, then crosses $x=0$ at about $t=5.24$ and moves towards Pattern B. By $t=20$, both preferences are approximately $+1.450$. These results agree with graphical analysis. With $I=0.70$, both starting preferences approach the same stable equilibrium, even though they initially favour different patterns.

![Comparison of two instruction conditions ($I=0$ and $I=0.70$)](figures/model_comparison.png){#fig-compare-models width=50%}


As shown in @fig-comapre-models, the positive instruction changes the number of stable equilibria from two to one. Without an instruction, the two starting preferences approach different stable equilibria. When $I=0$, the model has two stable states: one favouring Pattern A and one favouring Pattern B, separated by an unstable equilibrium at ($x=0$). With a positive instuction $I=0.70$, the stable equilibrium favouring Pattern A disappears, and ($x=0$) is no longer an equilibrium. Both starting preferences then approach the same stable equilibrium favouring Pattern B. The positive instruction therefore changes which stable preferences are possible in this model, allowing a preference that initially favours Pattern A to switch to Pattern B.
